claims.text: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimens, including an as-cast specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen, are the target material state.
Relevant electrical-conductivity measurements exist over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
A defect-aware, finite-temperature model will predict HfNbTaTiZr conductivity more accurately than analytical models based on perfect crystals.
The model will capture experimentally observed nonlinear temperature dependence in both specified temperature regimes.
The proposed framework explicitly represents point-defect scattering, lattice distortion, and temperature-dependent electron–phonon interactions.
Machine-learning or actively learned models can be combined with ab initio information and finite-temperature corrections in refractory multi-principal-element-alloy prediction workflows.
Oxygen in HfNbTaTiZr forms point defects that generate local lattice distortions and electron-scattering centers.
Lattice distortion can change the electronic characteristics and conductivity of high-entropy alloys.
Oxygen impurities induce localized electronic states and alter electron-scattering rates in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen-related scattering effects are more pronounced at cryogenic temperatures.
Oxygen defects influence weak localization in cryogenic HfNbTaTiZr.
At elevated temperatures, oxygen defects interfere with phonon-scattering dynamics.
Models that account for structural complexity should address limitations encountered when modeling HEA conductivity.
Defect-aware conductivity predictions will differ from defect-free analytical predictions by approximately 10–20%.
The model will reproduce nonlinear conductivity trends and possible activation-like behavior at high temperature.
The proposed applicability domain is bulk HfNbTaTiZr over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K, specifically benchmarked at 1 wt.% oxygen.
Predictions outside the specified temperature ranges or at other oxygen contents may be inaccurate.
Uncertainty in the predicted oxygen effect arises from defect-distribution complexity and temperature-dependent scattering rates.

The hypothesis is falsified if defect-free-model predictions agree with measured conductivity within their error margins and the defect-aware model provides no statistically significant accuracy improvement.
